interpretations.rationale: Mechanism. With Config.RestoreCommittedLogs set, NewRaft reads the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it before starting any background goroutine (api.go:723-754). processLogs delivers batches of at most config.MaxAppendEntries commit tuples through a select whose only other case is shutdownCh (raft.go:1302-1312), fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560), and its only consumer runFSM is started by api.go:636-638 after the replay returns, so ceil((commitIndex - lastApplied)/MaxAppendEntries) sends beyond 128 wait for a consumer that cannot exist until the blocked call finishes, with no timeout. Block. Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f restarts a single-voter prefix holding 9001 committed entries above an absent snapshot (event 16, 141 batches at MaxAppendEntries 64); the flag-on restart admitted by event 17 did not return within 8000ms (event 18) with the stack naming processLogs at raft.go:1346 called from restoreFromCommittedLogs at api.go:753 called from NewRaft, while the flag-off restart of the same shape returned in 5ms (event 21) and became leader (event 22); receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 reproduces both with return in 1ms. Bound. The revision of that harness adds a flag-on pair at MaxAppendEntries 16: 1501 replayed entries, 94 batches, returned in 0ms (event 25, comparison holds); 3001 entries, 188 batches, did not return (event 29, comparison violated, stack naming the same frames). Same flag, same batch size, same stores, only the replay volume differs, so the boundary sits between 94 and 128 batches, that is at 128 * MaxAppendEntries entries - 2048 at 16 and 8192 at the default 64. Availability. Receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a builds three voters at MaxAppendEntries 16, commits 3000 commands through a leader that is not A (event 9: A's staged commit index 3000, snapshot index 0, 188 batches), and restarts A in a goroutine. With the flag on the call did not return within 8000ms and the stack sample again names the replay frames (event 10), while the group kept committing with two members live (event 11: commit_while_two_live_ok true); stopping the member that is neither the leader nor A then left a single live member and the next command failed with 'leadership lost while committing log' (event 11: commit_after_stop_ok false). With the flag off, the same prefix and the same stop left the pair {leader, A} live and the command succeeded (events 13, 14: new_raft_returned true in 0ms, commit_after_stop_ok true). The only difference between the two cases is whether the restarted member came back, so the lost commit is attributable to the member that never started. Defect account: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft cannot complete startup whenever the committed log it replays needs more than 128 batches, that is more than 128*MaxAppendEntries entries above the restored snapshot index; at the default MaxAppendEntries of 64 that is 8192 entries and it is proportionally smaller for any smaller legal value, as measured at 16. The failure is a startup liveness failure: the node never begins participating, so a single-voter group stays down, and in a larger group the cluster keeps running on the remaining members with proportionally less fault tolerance - as observed, one member that could have started plus one deliberate stop is enough to make the group unable to commit. The pending operations the leader had accepted are answered with ErrLeadershipLost once it steps down (raft.go:508-528), which is the error text recorded in the witness.

knowledge.assertion: Each batch is delivered with a select between a send on fsmMutateCh and shutdownCh, so a full channel with no consumer waits indefinitely.
fsmMutateCh has capacity 128 and its consumer runFSM starts only after the startup replay returns.
The replay range above the snapshot sets the batch count, and the automatic snapshot cadence is the only bound on that range in a default deployment.
With the flag on, lastApplied is set to the persisted commit index before the replay, so the replay range spans the committed log above the snapshot.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize and the vote-admission checks, which is why a member that never starts is simply absent from every future majority.

counterevidence: The block itself is evidenced by non-return within an 8000ms window plus one stack sample per blocked case (events 18, 29 and 10). The permanence argument does not rest on those samples: the source shows no timeout, a single consumer started only after the blocked call returns, and an escape requiring an object the caller has not received. The flag-off controls return in 0, 1 and 5 ms across the receipts (events 21, 25 and 13).

The measured bound comes from two batch sizes and one replay per side, so the boundary is bracketed between 94 and 128 batches rather than binary-searched; the arithmetic form of the bound is supported by the source, and a registration between the two would be needed to place the edge exactly.

With the default SnapshotThreshold of 8192 equal to the default bound, a default node blocks only when the committed range above its newest snapshot exceeds 8192; every case here raised SnapshotThreshold, a legal Config field, so how readily a default deployment crosses the bound is not measured.

The availability case contains a deliberate second stop, so what it shows is the loss of the group's fault-tolerance margin rather than an outage in an untouched cluster; the control with the replay disabled performs the same stop and still commits, which is what attributes the loss to the member that did not return.

In the flag-on case the surviving leader's command failed with 'leadership lost while committing log', which is the leader stepping down and failing its pending operations rather than a defect of its own. The same apply succeeded while two members were live (event 11, commit_while_two_live_ok true) and succeeded after the same stop in the control (event 14), so the failure is attributable to the missing quorum.

The blocked NewRaft call is abandoned in a separate goroutine so the test can complete; that is a harness choice, not a repair, and the harness never observes the process-level consequence of a caller that waits forever.
limitations: All nodes are in-memory transports and stores in one process with a test commit-tracking store; no production store and no process-level restart are exercised, and the confined goroutine is the only trace of the real caller's hang.

interpretations.rationale: Correction account, needed because the earlier interpretations of this question stated the reachable replay in replayed log entries. Source: processLogs appends a commit tuple only for entries prepareLog accepts - LogCommand and LogBarrier always, LogConfiguration only when protocolVersion > 2 - and none for LogNoop or the deprecated peer entries, and it flushes a batch when the batch reaches config.MaxAppendEntries (raft.go:1296-1364, prepareLog at raft.go:1364-1391). The delivered batch count is therefore ceil(tuples/MaxAppendEntries) for the tuples in the replayed range, and a count computed from the range's index span is an upper bound that can be loose when the range contains entries that produce no tuple. Corroboration from the retained boundary receipt 8a710c75d1814aafad5d24b536998539 (cited as non-supporting corroboration, since this account makes no defect judgment): the prefix whose replayed range ends at index 2049 spans 2049 entries but contains 2048 tuples, delivered as 128 batches (event 31), and NewRaft returned in 0ms (event 32); the prefix ending at 2050 contains 2049 tuples, delivered as 129 batches (event 34), and NewRaft did not return within 8000ms (event 35, three stack mentions naming the replay frames). The entry-based figure the harness computes for the returning case also reads 129 batches, which is exactly the overstatement the correction describes. What does not change: the mechanism (a full 128-slot channel whose only consumer starts after the replay returns, with no timeout), the fact that the replay is bounded by the committed range above the restored snapshot, and the consequences already recorded, since command-dominated logs deliver close to one tuple per entry. What changes: the exact threshold should be stated in delivered batches - 128 * MaxAppendEntries tuples, 8192 at the default MaxAppendEntries of 64 - and a bound stated in log entries is an upper bound rather than an equality, with the gap widening on logs that carry no-op entries or, below protocol version 3, configuration entries.

3bdf46ca8b274b719cc26e672b951e75-gap-2.explanation: The corrected unit is commit tuples. prepareLog decides it: commands and barriers always produce a tuple, configuration entries only above protocol version 2, and no-op and deprecated peer entries never do (raft.go:1364-1391), while processLogs flushes a batch when the accumulated tuples reach MaxAppendEntries (raft.go:1336-1350). So the number of sends is ceil(tuples/MaxAppendEntries), and any figure derived from a log index range is an upper bound on that number.

3bdf46ca8b274b719cc26e672b951e75-gap-3.explanation: The retained boundary receipt shows the correction in an observation rather than only in the source: a replayed range of 2049 entries ending at index 2049 held 2048 tuples and was delivered as 128 batches, and NewRaft returned in 0ms (events 31, 32), while the range ending at 2050 held 2049 tuples and 129 batches and did not return (events 34, 35). The entry-based count the harness computes reads 129 in the returning case as well, which is the overstatement the correction names.

3bdf46ca8b274b719cc26e672b951e75-gap-4.explanation: For the earlier interpretations, the change is one of precision rather than of substance: their threshold expressions in replayed entries remain upper bounds, valid where the replayed range is dominated by commands and configuration entries at protocol 3 or above, and the mechanism, the 128-slot channel, the observable block and its consequences are unaffected. The successor account for this question states the bound in delivered batches and cites the batching behaviour at revision 2, so the recorded conclusion no longer rests on the entry-based phrasing.

The correction widens in the other direction too: below protocol version 3 the replayed range can contain many configuration entries that produce no tuple, so an entry-based threshold can overstate the reachable batch count by far more than the one or two entries seen at protocol 3, while the mechanism and its consequences are unchanged.
This account makes no defect judgment of its own; the defect account for this question remains the experiment-cited interpretation, whose conclusion is unaffected by the counting unit.

That state decides election eligibility (raft.go:225-246), quorum size (raft.go:1085-1094), the leader's commitment membership (raft.go:456-467, commitment.go:35-64) and vote admission. First consequence: receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a removed server C from {A,B,C} (event 2: committed configuration at index 5 with two voters), restarted A with the flag on while B was partitioned, and A tracked the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration containing C (event 3); A won the election counting C and committed 'stale-quorum-entry' at index 10 term 4 with apply_error null, its FSM applied it, B's log lacked that index and C's log held it at the same term (event 4). Since A's own match cannot form a majority of three and B had no transport path, the deciding acknowledgement can only have come from C: the entry was committed, applied and reported successful against a member set that is not a majority of the committed configuration. Second consequence, durable: receipt c477da09810f4842ba55130320e2a6b5 leaves A in that recovered state on a three-voter cluster (event 6: latest_config_index 0 with no members and committed_config_index 0, against its log's index-1 three-voter entry and staged commit index 4), takes a snapshot through the library's normal path, and reads back metadata recording no configuration at index 0 while the log establishes a three-voter configuration at index 1 (event 7, snapshot_config_matches_log_config false). A then restarts on the same stores with the replay disabled and comes up with an empty configuration at index 0, no leader within 1500ms, in state Follower (event 8). The loss is therefore not confined to the replay path: once written, the snapshot metadata re-imposes it on a restart that never enables the feature. Defect account: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a commit-tracking log store, NewRaft cannot roll the node's tracked membership configuration forward past max(snapshot index, persisted commit index), so the node may keep an older or empty membership although its own log already contains the committed configuration entries; the recovered node can be permanently unable to participate, can decide leadership and commit index from a member set the committed configuration does not match - committing an entry a real voter of that configuration does not hold - and can write the lost configuration into durable snapshot metadata, from which later restarts, including ones with the feature disabled, restore it. The library's own test for the feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration already equals the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this path. knowledge.assertion: The startup configuration scan runs from max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1, so entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry at startup.

processConfigurationLogEntry is the only writer of the tracked configuration state; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into it.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership, leader-lease voter counting and the vote-admission checks.
A follower with configurations.latestIndex equal to 0 does not start an election, which is terminal when no reachable peer can supply a configuration entry.
Snapshots record the committed configuration and its index that the node currently tracks, and startup restores that metadata into the tracked configuration.

Block and bound. Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f restarts a single-voter prefix holding 9001 committed entries above an absent snapshot (event 16, 141 delivered batches at MaxAppendEntries 64); the flag-on restart admitted by event 17 did not return within 8000ms (event 18, stack naming processLogs at raft.go:1346 called from restoreFromCommittedLogs at api.go:753 called from NewRaft) while the flag-off restart of the same shape returned in 1ms (event 21) and became leader (event 22); receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 reproduces both, with its own flag-off control returning in 5ms (its event 21) and adds a pair at MaxAppendEntries 16 where 1501 replayed entries (94 batches) returned in 0ms (event 25) and 3001 entries (188 batches) did not (event 29). interpretations.rationale: Extension note: this successor adds receipt 4178d9d5c479470cafb7ebd7951a9332, which observes in a three-voter group that a node recovering without a configuration never attempts candidacy while the same node and log with the replay disabled do; the sources, the three earlier executions, the knowledge uses, the conclusion and the remaining counterevidence are otherwise unchanged, and the counter about the observation window is strengthened with the new control's sample counts. Correction note: this successor differs from the previous account of this question only by a transcribed latency; the control's election is now stated as the receipt records it (19 polls at a 5ms interval, about 95ms), not from an earlier construction run. Everything else - sources, executions, knowledge uses, counterevidence and limitations - is unchanged. Recovery. Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c restarted four real single-voter prefixes on their retained stores with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off: with the flag on and no snapshot the node recovered an empty configuration (event 2: no members at index 0, 268 polls without a leader) although its log holds the bootstrap configuration entry at index 1 (event 0), the flag-off control on the same prefix shape tracked that entry and elected itself (event 6), and with a snapshot taken before a committed AddNonvoter the flag-on node kept the snapshot's index-1 configuration instead of the log's committed index-7 configuration (events 10, 11) while the flag-off control recovered index 7 (event 15). Source side the mechanism is settled: restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754), advancing lastApplied before NewRaft runs the scan that rebuilds tracked configuration state from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 (api.go:602-621), so committed configuration entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go:1605-1624) and the FSM's ConfigurationStore is never read back. That state decides election eligibility (raft.go:225-246), quorum size (raft.go:1085-1094), the leader's commitment membership (raft.go:456-467, commitment.go:35-64) and vote admission. First consequence: receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a removed server C from {A,B,C} (event 2: committed configuration at index 5 with two voters), restarted A with the flag on while B was partitioned, and A tracked the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration containing C (event 3); A won the election counting C and committed 'stale-quorum-entry' at index 10 term 4 with apply_error null, its FSM applied it, B's log lacked that index and C's log held it at the same term (event 4). Since A's own match cannot form a majority of three and B had no transport path, the deciding acknowledgement can only have come from C: the entry was committed, applied and reported successful against a member set that is not a majority of the committed configuration. Authority attempt. Receipt 4178d9d5c479470cafb7ebd7951a9332 builds a three-voter group, commits three commands so the staged commit index is non-zero, restarts A over its own stores and reads its tracked configuration: with the replay enabled A tracks no configuration at all (event 15: latest_config_index 0, no members, staged commit index 4), and in 266 samples over 1500ms of hearing no leader with the other voters shut down it was a follower in every sample and never a candidate (event 16, comparison violated); with the replay disabled the same node and the same log recover the three-voter configuration (event 17: latest_config_index 1, three members) and the node was a candidate in 254 of 266 samples, ending in state Candidate (event 18, comparison holds). A node whose tracked configuration is empty therefore does not merely fail to win an election: it never attempts to acquire authority, so it cannot be the source of a new leader even when the surviving members could form a quorum with it. Second consequence, durable: receipt c477da09810f4842ba55130320e2a6b5 leaves A in that recovered state on a three-voter cluster (event 6: latest_config_index 0 with no members and committed_config_index 0, against its log's index-1 three-voter entry and staged commit index 4), takes a snapshot through the library's normal path, and reads back metadata recording no configuration at index 0 while the log establishes a three-voter configuration at index 1 (event 7, snapshot_config_matches_log_config false). A then restarts on the same stores with the replay disabled and comes up with an empty configuration at index 0, no leader within 1500ms, in state Follower (event 8). The loss is therefore not confined to the replay path: once written, the snapshot metadata re-imposes it on a restart that never enables the feature. Defect account: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a commit-tracking log store, NewRaft cannot roll the node's tracked membership configuration forward past max(snapshot index, persisted commit index), so the node may keep an older or empty membership although its own log already contains the committed configuration entries; the recovered node can be permanently unable to participate, can decide leadership and commit index from a member set the committed configuration does not match - committing an entry a real voter of that configuration does not hold - and can write the lost configuration into durable snapshot metadata, from which later restarts, including ones with the feature disabled, restore it. The library's own test for the feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration already equals the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this path. The failed first execution of the multi-node experiment (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469, exit 1) is retained in the run's logs but is not cited as an execution here: it stopped in the harness at the snapshot step because the elected leader was not the node being snapshotted, so it produced no comparison result about the target.

knowledge.assertion: The startup configuration scan runs from max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1, so entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry at startup.
restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the store's commit index and calls processLogs with it only when the flag is set, which advances lastApplied to that index before the scan runs.
processConfigurationLogEntry is the only writer of the tracked configuration state; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into it.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership, leader-lease voter counting and the vote-admission checks.
A follower with configurations.latestIndex equal to 0 does not start an election, which is terminal when no reachable peer can supply a configuration entry.
Snapshots record the committed configuration and its index that the node currently tracks, and startup restores that metadata into the tracked configuration.

counterevidence: The doc comment for RestoreCommittedLogs (config.go:243-254) promises only that committed logs are replayed to catch the FSM up and says nothing about membership recovery, so the stale tracked configuration can be read as an unnamed side effect of a feature that never claimed to preserve it. The counter is that the startup scan at api.go:610-621 exists to rebuild that state from the log, and the observed consequences are a commit decided against a member set the committed configuration does not contain and a durable record that re-imposes the loss.

The commit-rule violation needs the removed server C to stay reachable after its removal, since its acknowledgement is what the stale majority counted; if it were stopped or unreachable the same stale configuration would instead leave the node unable to commit. The receipt therefore shows one reachable-removed-server case rather than every case.

One could argue the snapshot in the durable-state case is only as good as the state the node tracks, and that a caller should not snapshot a node whose configuration is empty. The counter is that the node is an ordinary cluster member whose own log contains the configuration entries, nothing in the API or the documentation marks its snapshots as unusable, and the resulting metadata then defeats a restart that has the feature disabled, so the corruption outlives the condition that created it.

The flag-off restart's failure to lead could be attributed to the 1500ms observation window rather than to the empty configuration. The counter is the source guard that refuses elections while configurations.latestIndex is zero (raft.go:225-241) plus two controls inside the same window: the single-voter control elected itself in 19 polls of the harness's 5ms interval (receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c, event 6), and in the authority case the node that recovered its configuration was a candidate in 254 of 266 samples while the node with the empty configuration showed zero candidate samples (receipt 4178d9d5c479470cafb7ebd7951a9332, events 16 and 18).

The harness assigns roles deliberately (A restarts, B is partitioned, leadership is moved with the library's transfer) and it takes the snapshot explicitly rather than through the automatic cadence. Those choices select the scenario but do not supply the stale or empty configuration, which event 6 shows against the node's own log, nor the acknowledgement, which C's log carries.

The first execution of the multi-node experiment failed in the harness before any comparison (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469) and is retained as a harness artifact; the later receipts contain the same scenario with both defects exercised.

The authority case removes the other voters by shutting them down, so it shows that the defective node never attempts candidacy; it does not show an outage that a correct recovery would have prevented, because the recovered three-voter configuration also lacks a quorum with one voter left. What the receipt adds is the capability difference, not a counterfactual outage.
limitations: All nodes are in-memory transports and stores in one process and the harness uses a test log store whose staging is not atomic with its log writes; the caller-side durability contract of CommitTrackingLogStore is assumed, not verified, and no production store or snapshot store is exercised.

The durable-state case snapshots a node that has no snapshot on its stores and then restarts with the replay disabled; shipping such a snapshot to a follower, or corruption arising from the automatic snapshot cadence, is not exercised, and deleting the corrupt snapshot is not tested as a recovery.

The multi-node case is one prefix shape with one committed removal, keeps the removed server running, and injects no message loss, reordering or crash, so the decision defect is observed under a clean transport.

Receipt 4178d9d5c479470cafb7ebd7951a9332 builds a three-voter group, commits three commands so the staged commit index is non-zero, restarts A over its own stores and reads its tracked configuration: with the replay enabled A tracks no configuration at all (event 15: latest_config_index 0, no members, staged commit index 4), and in 266 samples over 1500ms of hearing no leader with the other voters shut down it was a follower in every sample and never a candidate (event 16, comparison violated); with the replay disabled the same node and the same log recover the three-voter configuration (event 17: latest_config_index 1, three members) and the node was a candidate in 254 of 266 samples, ending in state Candidate (event 18, comparison holds). restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the store's commit index and calls processLogs with it only when the flag is set, which advances lastApplied to that index before the scan runs.
processConfigurationLogEntry is the only writer of the tracked configuration state; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into it.

A follower with configurations.latestIndex equal to 0 does not start an election, which is terminal when no reachable peer can supply a configuration entry.

The commit-rule violation needs the removed server C to stay reachable after its removal, since its acknowledgement is what the stale majority counted; if it were stopped or unreachable the same stale configuration would instead leave the node unable to commit. The receipt therefore shows one reachable-removed-server case rather than every case.

One could argue the snapshot in the durable-state case is only as good as the state the node tracks, and that a caller should not snapshot a node whose configuration is empty. The counter is that the node is an ordinary cluster member whose own log contains the configuration entries, nothing in the API or the documentation marks its snapshots as unusable, and the resulting metadata then defeats a restart that has the feature disabled, so the corruption outlives the condition that created it.

The flag-off restart's failure to lead could be attributed to the 1500ms observation window rather than to the empty configuration. Schedule variation is limited: the multi-node scenario appears in two receipts with the same operands, the durable-state scenario in one, and the observation windows are 1500ms for non-participation and 2000ms apply timeouts.

The harness assigns roles deliberately (A restarts, B is partitioned, leadership is moved with the library's transfer) and it takes the snapshot explicitly rather than through the automatic cadence. The first execution of the multi-node experiment failed in the harness before any comparison (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469) and is retained as a harness artifact; the later receipts contain the same scenario with both defects exercised.

The authority witness depends on a property of the caller's store: A's persisted commit index must be non-zero, because that value becomes lastApplied and pushes the startup scan above the log's configuration entry. Precision note: the entry-based batch figures recorded by the earlier receipts equal the delivered counts there, and the receipts' own operands show why. In receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f event 16 the prefix ends at log index 9002 with staged commit index 9001, so the replayed range holds the bootstrap configuration entry, one no-op and 8999 commands, that is 9000 tuples, and ceil(9000/64) = 141, the figure the receipt records for that case. Receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 records 1501 and 3001 replayed entries with 94 and 188 batches at MaxAppendEntries 16, and the same counting gives 1500 and 3000 tuples, ceil(1500/16) = 94 and ceil(3000/16) = 188. The two counts diverge only where the replayed range ends inside a batch in a way that adds a no-op, which is what the boundary receipt's 2049-entry range with 128 delivered batches shows. A citation check of this account against the retained observations found no other discrepancy. Correction note: this successor extends the previous account of this question with the default-configuration receipt; sources, the earlier executions, knowledge uses, conclusions and limitations are otherwise unchanged, and the counterevidence item that recorded default-cadence reachability as unmeasured is replaced by the measured statement. Correction note: this successor differs from the previous account of this question only in two transcribed numbers and their attribution; the flag-off control of receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f returned in 1ms and the same control of receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 returned in 5ms, as those receipts record, and the earlier account had them swapped. Everything else - sources, executions, knowledge uses, counterevidence, limitations and joint history - is unchanged. Mechanism. With Config.RestoreCommittedLogs set, NewRaft reads the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it before starting any background goroutine (api.go:723-754). processLogs walks the committed range and appends a commit tuple only for entries prepareLog accepts - commands and barriers always, configuration entries when protocolVersion > 2, and nothing for no-op or deprecated peer entries - flushing a batch whenever the batch reaches config.MaxAppendEntries and delivering it through a select whose only other case is shutdownCh (raft.go:1296-1364 with prepareLog at raft.go:1364-1391). fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560) and its only consumer runFSM is started by api.go:636-638 after the replay returns, so a replay needing more than 128 delivered batches waits for a consumer that cannot exist until the blocked call finishes, with no timeout. Block and bound. Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f restarts a single-voter prefix holding 9001 committed entries above an absent snapshot (event 16, 141 delivered batches at MaxAppendEntries 64); the flag-on restart admitted by event 17 did not return within 8000ms (event 18, stack naming processLogs at raft.go:1346 called from restoreFromCommittedLogs at api.go:753 called from NewRaft) while the flag-off restart of the same shape returned in 1ms (event 21) and became leader (event 22); receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 reproduces both, with its own flag-off control returning in 5ms (its event 21) and adds a pair at MaxAppendEntries 16 where 1501 replayed entries (94 batches) returned in 0ms (event 25) and 3001 entries (188 batches) did not (event 29). Receipt 8a710c75d1814aafad5d24b536998539 then places the boundary exactly: at MaxAppendEntries 16 one prefix ends at staged commit index 2049, whose replayed range contains 2048 entries that become commit tuples, that is 128 delivered batches (event 31), and NewRaft returned in 0ms (event 32, comparison holds); the other ends at 2050 with 2049 tuples, that is 129 delivered batches (event 34), and NewRaft did not return within 8000ms (event 35, comparison violated, three stack mentions naming the replay frames). Default configuration. Receipt 0cb30b6bf8874d479b83653bd4e6c553 builds two further single-voter prefixes with Config.DefaultConfig values left untouched: event 36 records SnapshotThreshold 8192, MaxAppendEntries 64, SnapshotInterval 120s, 12000 applied commands, staged commit index 12001, snapshot index 0, no snapshots listed, and a committed range of 12001 entries above the snapshot against the bound of 128*64 = 8192 tuples; the flag-on restart did not return within 8000ms with four stack samples naming the replay frames (event 38, comparison violated), while the flag-off control returned in 3ms (event 41, comparison holds). The trigger therefore needs no tuning of threshold or batch size: the automatic snapshot loop wakes on a randomized timeout of up to SnapshotInterval (snapshot.go:71-95), so a node that commits faster than that cadence carries a range above the bound into its restart. Availability. Receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a builds three voters at MaxAppendEntries 16, commits 3000 commands through a leader that is not A (event 9), restarts A in a goroutine, and observes the same non-return (event 10). The corrected unit matters for the recorded gaps: the three correction gaps ask about the premise change, and the receipt answers them substantively - the returning case's entry-based figure was 129 batches while only 128 were delivered, so counts derived from a log index range are upper bounds. Defect account: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft cannot complete startup whenever the replay delivers more than 128 batches, that is more than 128*MaxAppendEntries entries that become commit tuples above the restored snapshot index; at the default MaxAppendEntries of 64 that is 8192 tuples, and it is proportionally smaller for any smaller legal value, as measured at 16 (2048 tuples returning, 2049 blocking). knowledge.assertion: Batches are counted in commit tuples, so no-op and deprecated peer entries consume no batch slot and configuration entries do so only above protocol version 2.
fsmMutateCh has capacity 128 and its consumer runFSM starts only after the startup replay returns.
The replay range above the snapshot sets the number of tuples to deliver, and the automatic snapshot cadence is the only bound on that range in a default deployment.
With the flag on, lastApplied is set to the persisted commit index before the replay, so the replay range spans the committed log above the snapshot.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize and the vote-admission checks, which is why a member that never starts is simply absent from every future majority.

counterevidence: The block itself is evidenced by non-return within an 8000ms window plus a stack sample per blocked case (events 18, 29, 10 and 35). The permanence argument does not rest on those samples: the source shows no timeout, a single consumer started only after the blocked call returns, and an escape requiring an object the caller has not received. The flag-off controls return promptly in each receipt: 1ms at event 21 of receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f, 5ms at event 21 and 0ms at event 25 of receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00, and 0ms at event 13 of receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a.

The boundary pair has now been executed twice from the same fixed inputs in separate clean copies with identical operands (receipts 8a710c75d1814aafad5d24b536998539 and 9039d268ffc24fa085efc75de7dc4fb2), but its delivered-tuple count is computed by the harness scanning the replayed range with the same type rule prepareLog uses rather than read from an internal counter; the behaviour straddles the boundary by one replayed command, and the tuple figure is an inspectable operand rather than the decisive predicate.

The default-configuration case is a burst: the harness applies commands as fast as the in-memory stack allows and no automatic snapshot had fired at restart (event 36: snapshot index 0, no snapshots listed). It reproduced identically in the second execution of the same fixed experiment (receipt 9039d268ffc24fa085efc75de7dc4fb2, events 36 to 41). It shows that default settings do not keep the range below the bound during a burst, not how long a node typically stays above it, and the other cases that raised SnapshotThreshold made the condition permanent rather than momentary.

The availability case contains a deliberate second stop, so what it shows is the loss of the group's fault-tolerance margin rather than an outage in an untouched cluster; the control with the replay disabled performs the same stop and still commits, which is what attributes the loss to the member that did not return.

In the flag-on availability case the surviving leader's command failed with 'leadership lost while committing log', which is the leader stepping down and failing its pending operations rather than a defect of its own; the same apply succeeded while two members were live (event 11) and after the same stop in the control (event 14).

The blocked NewRaft call is abandoned in a separate goroutine so the tests can complete; that is a harness choice, not a repair, and no harness observes the process-level consequence of a caller that waits forever.
limitations: All cases run in one process over in-memory transports and a test commit-tracking store; no production store, no process-level restart and no disk fault are exercised, and the confined goroutine is the only trace of the real caller's hang.

The availability case uses one prefix shape, one batch size (16) and one extra stop; the boundary case uses one batch size and one run per side; observation windows are 8000ms for restarts and 3000ms for the applies.

Schedule variation is unevenly covered: the original 9000-entry pair appears in two receipts, the boundary pair and the default-configuration pair have each been executed twice from the same fixed inputs with identical operands, while the bound pair remains single-run and the availability pair has now been executed three times with the same split; each blocked state is still sampled once per execution.
The bound's dependence on the caller-side store is assumed rather than verified: the replay range comes from the stored commit index, whose durability contract belongs to the LogStore implementation.

It shows that default settings do not keep the range below the bound during a burst, not how long a node typically stays above it, and the other cases that raised SnapshotThreshold made the condition permanent rather than momentary.

The availability case contains a deliberate second stop, so what it shows is the loss of the group's fault-tolerance margin rather than an outage in an untouched cluster; the control with the replay disabled performs the same stop and still commits, which is what attributes the loss to the member that did not return.

In the flag-on availability case the surviving leader's command failed with 'leadership lost while committing log', which is the leader stepping down and failing its pending operations rather than a defect of its own; the same apply succeeded while two members were live (event 11) and after the same stop in the control (event 14).

The blocked NewRaft call is abandoned in a separate goroutine so the tests can complete; that is a harness choice, not a repair, and no harness observes the process-level consequence of a caller that waits forever.
limitations: All cases run in one process over in-memory transports and a test commit-tracking store; no production store, no process-level restart and no disk fault are exercised, and the confined goroutine is the only trace of the real caller's hang.

The availability case uses one prefix shape, one batch size (16) and one extra stop; the boundary case uses one batch size and one run per side; observation windows are 8000ms for restarts and 3000ms for the applies.

Schedule variation is unevenly covered: the original 9000-entry pair appears in two receipts, the boundary pair and the default-configuration pair have each been executed twice from the same fixed inputs with identical operands, the bound pair has now been executed twice with identical operands, and the availability pair three times with the same split; each blocked state is still sampled once per execution.
The bound's dependence on the caller-side store is assumed rather than verified: the replay range comes from the stored commit index, whose durability contract belongs to the LogStore implementation.
interpretations.joint_history: All four receipts are executions of fixed experiments for this investigation on the same captured source revision, in separate workspaces with no shared mutable state, and their harnesses share the same initialization: an in-memory commit-tracking log store, a single-voter bootstrap for the first three, RestoreCommittedLogs enabled on the prefix, and the restart in a separate goroutine with an 8000ms window. Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f and its revision e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 use one harness whose cases differ only in Config.MaxAppendEntries and the committed range, and e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 re-runs the original 9000-entry pair unchanged. Receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a uses a three-voter harness at the same MaxAppendEntries 16 and observes the same block. Receipt 8a710c75d1814aafad5d24b536998539 uses the first harness's prefix construction with targets chosen from an earlier construction run of the same case and places the replay on both sides of the channel capacity. The blocked state in every receipt is corroborated by a stack sample naming the replay frames, and no receipt depends on another's runtime state. result.summary: Corrected a recorded premise that my own newest evidence refines. Knowledge 29e4214f5ee146b393957fa23a33a73d-knowledge-2 previously said the automatic snapshot cadence keeps the committed range above the snapshot near SnapshotThreshold; the default-configuration receipt measures 12001 entries above an absent snapshot with the threshold at 8192 and no snapshot taken (receipt 0cb30b6bf8874d479b83653bd4e6c553, event 36), because runSnapshots evaluates shouldSnapshot only when a randomized timeout of up to SnapshotInterval expires (snapshot.go:71-95). Revision 2 states that the range can pass the threshold and keep growing between checks, with the defaults spelled out; the correction lists the seven interpretation IDs that relied on the earlier wording as affected uses, which the controller propagates to the investigation. The replay-completion account gained a successor interpretation that cites the corrected revision, opens with a correction note explaining the measured margin and why it differs from 'near the threshold', and leaves its executions, conclusion, counterevidence (including the burst-workload caveat) and limitations unchanged. Both this and the configuration-recovery account's remaining limitations are structural to the harness rather than statements my evidence contradicts.

investigations.question: When Config.RestoreCommittedLogs is enabled, does NewRaft recover the membership configuration that the node's own log already contains, and what does the recovered node then do with the configuration-dependent decisions (election eligibility and quorum membership) that follow?
investigations.hypothesis: restoreFromCommittedLogs sets lastApplied to the persisted commit index before the startup configuration scan, so the scan begins above every configuration entry at an index <= that commit index. The node keeps the snapshot's committed configuration, or an empty configuration when it has no snapshot, even though its log holds newer committed configuration entries. Because that configuration state decides election eligibility, quorumSize, and the membership used by the leader's commitment, the recovery can leave a node unable to participate, and it can leave a node that can win an election counting quorum from a stale member set.
investigations.discriminator: Restart two identically built real prefixes on top of the same stores: one with RestoreCommittedLogs on and one with it off. Compare the recovered configuration (index, voter/nonvoter membership) against the newest configuration entry in the node's own log, and whether the node reaches leadership within a fixed window.

gaps.question: Which startup inputs are permitted to establish the node's tracked configuration: the log scan, the snapshot metadata, and the restored FSM are separate sources, and only some of them write r.configurations. Which one is authoritative for a restart with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled?

Does a recovered stale or empty configuration view change a decision that is observable outside the node - an election it wins, a vote it grants, or a commit index it advances using a quorum that the actual committed configuration does not contain?

investigations.question: Can the startup replay that Config.RestoreCommittedLogs performs fail to complete? restoreFromCommittedLogs applies committed entries through processLogs before NewRaft starts the FSM goroutine, and processLogs hands each batch to a fixed-capacity channel, so the completion of NewRaft may depend on how much committed log lies above the snapshot.
investigations.hypothesis: processLogs sends each batch of at most MaxAppendEntries commit tuples to fsmMutateCh, a buffered channel created with capacity 128 whose only consumer is runFSM, started only after restoreFromCommittedLogs returns, and the send blocks until buffer space appears or shutdownCh closes. A replay containing more than 128 batches therefore blocks inside NewRaft, before the consumer exists and before any goroutine that could report an error runs; since NewRaft has not returned, no caller can close shutdownCh, so the send is not merely slow but unrepairable from within the process. The number of batches is ceil((commitIndex - lastApplied)/MaxAppendEntries), and at startup with the flag on lastApplied is the restored snapshot index, so the trigger is a committed log more than 128*MaxAppendEntries above the snapshot: 8192 entries with the default MaxAppendEntries of 64, which is the same order as the default SnapshotThreshold of 8192, and proportionally less with any smaller legal MaxAppendEntries.
investigations.discriminator: Build prefixes whose committed log lies far above an absent snapshot, then restart them with RestoreCommittedLogs on and off. If the replay volume alone were the problem, both restarts would stall or both would finish; if the ordering of the replay against the FSM consumer is the problem, only the flag-on restart fails to return, and a stack sample of the blocked goroutine names the replay frames.

knowledge.statement: NewRaft rebuilds configuration state by iterating log indices from max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied) + 1 up to the last log index and calling processConfigurationLogEntry for each entry; entries at or below max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied) are never passed to that function during startup.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to every NewRaft call, before the background goroutines start (api.go:602-621).

knowledge.statement: When and only when Config.RestoreCommittedLogs is set, NewRaft calls restoreFromCommittedLogs: it reads CommitTrackingLogStore.GetCommitIndex, clamps it to the store's last index, stores it as the node's commit index, and calls processLogs with it, which advances lastApplied to that index (index <= lastApplied returns early without applying).
knowledge.conditions: Requires the log store to implement CommitTrackingLogStore; otherwise NewRaft fails with ErrIncompatibleLogStore (api.go:723-754, log.go:194-215).

knowledge.statement: processConfigurationLogEntry is the only writer of r.configurations.latest/committed for LogConfiguration and deprecated peer entries; its callers are appendEntries for newly appended entries and the NewRaft startup scan. Applying a committed configuration entry to the FSM (runFSM -> FSM.Apply or ConfigurationStore.StoreConfiguration) does not write r.configurations.
knowledge.conditions: LogConfiguration entries are passed to the FSM as commit tuples when protocolVersion > 2, so FSM-side configuration storage is independent of the node's tracked configuration state.

knowledge.statement: The node's tracked latest configuration is the sole input to quorumSize(), to the voter counting in checkLeaderLease, to the membership map built by newCommitment/setConfiguration for the leader's commit index, and to the inConfiguration/hasVote admission checks that decide vote and pre-vote grants.
knowledge.conditions: Holds for a leader and during elections; the leader builds its commitment from r.configurations.latest at leader setup and on each committed configuration change (raft.go:456-467, 1085-1094; commitment.go:35-64).

knowledge.statement: On heartbeat timeout a follower avoids starting an election when configurations.latestIndex == 0 (logs 'no known peers, aborting election'), and when the latest configuration is already committed and does not contain the local node as a voter; a node without voters in its tracked configuration therefore stays in the follower state indefinitely unless a newer configuration entry arrives.
knowledge.conditions: Observed on the follower heartbeat-timeout branch; with no reachable peers, nothing else can change the tracked configuration (raft.go:225-246).

knowledge.statement: The commit index is written to a commit-tracking log store only through tryStageCommitIndex, which returns immediately when RestoreCommittedLogs is not set; it is called before StoreLogs in dispatchLogs (leader) and before StoreLogs of newly received entries in appendEntries (follower).
knowledge.conditions: So a prefix that never enabled RestoreCommittedLogs has no staged commit index for a later restart to read (raft.go:1392-1405, 1553-1561).

knowledge.statement: processLogs walks the committed range from lastApplied+1 to the given index, appends a commit tuple only for entries prepareLog accepts (LogCommand and LogBarrier always, LogConfiguration when protocolVersion > 2; LogNoop and the deprecated peer entries produce none), flushes a batch whenever the batch reaches config.MaxAppendEntries, and delivers each batch with a select whose only cases are a send on r.fsmMutateCh and a receive on r.shutdownCh; when the channel has no free slot and the node is not shutting down, the send waits indefinitely.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to every caller of processLogs: the startup replay in restoreFromCommittedLogs, the leader commit path and the follower AppendEntries path (raft.go:1296-1364 with prepareLog at raft.go:1364-1391).

history.statement: processLogs applies committed entries in batches of at most config.MaxAppendEntries and delivers each batch with a select whose only cases are a send on r.fsmMutateCh and a receive on r.shutdownCh; when the channel has no free slot and the node is not shutting down, the send waits indefinitely.
history.conditions: Applies to every caller of processLogs, including the startup replay in restoreFromCommittedLogs and the leader and follower apply paths (raft.go:1296-1364).

No-op entries consume no batch slot, and configuration entries do so only above protocol version 2, so any batch count computed from a log index range is an upper bound.

knowledge.statement: fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 in NewRaft's struct literal, and its consumer runFSM is started with r.goFunc(r.runFSM) only after restoreSnapshot, restoreFromCommittedLogs and the configuration scan have all returned; nothing else consumes fsmMutateCh.
knowledge.conditions: During NewRaft the channel has no consumer at all, so a replay requiring more than 128 batch sends cannot make progress (api.go:555-562, 628-640).

knowledge.statement: shouldSnapshot returns true once the log's last index minus the last snapshot index reaches config.SnapshotThreshold, but runSnapshots evaluates it only when a randomized timeout of up to config.SnapshotInterval expires, so between checks the committed range above the newest snapshot can exceed the threshold by a wide margin; with the defaults (threshold 8192, MaxAppendEntries 64, SnapshotInterval 120s) a node that commits faster than that cadence carries a range above the bound into its restart.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the automatic snapshot loop on every node; the threshold compares the log store's last index with the last snapshot index, not the applied index (snapshot.go:71-121, config.go:331-342).

history.statement: shouldSnapshot triggers when the log's last index minus the last snapshot index reaches config.SnapshotThreshold (default 8192, with MaxAppendEntries default 64 and SnapshotInterval default 120s), so the automatic snapshot cadence normally keeps the committed range above the snapshot near that threshold, and a store that keeps its log without snapshotting is not bounded by it.

knowledge.statement: takeSnapshot reads the configurations tracked by the main thread and passes the committed configuration and its committed index into SnapshotStore.Create, so the snapshot metadata is only as correct as the configuration state the node currently tracks; restoreSnapshot installs that same configuration and index into both committed and latest on startup, and the startup scan then starts above max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied).
knowledge.conditions: Applies to user and automatic snapshots on any node state, and to every startup that restores a snapshot (snapshot.go:155-190, api.go:653-684).

interpretations.rationale: Source trace. NewRaft restores the newest usable snapshot, then, only with RestoreCommittedLogs, reads the persisted commit index from the commit-tracking log store, stores it and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754); processLogs sets lastApplied to that index (raft.go:1296-1364). Only after that does NewRaft run the scan that rebuilds the node's configuration from the log, and that scan starts at max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied) + 1 (api.go:602-621). With the feature off, lastApplied equals the snapshot index, so the scan covers every configuration entry in the log; with the feature on, lastApplied is the commit index, which for a node that committed entries above its newest snapshot is strictly larger, so every configuration entry at an index <= that commit index is skipped even though it is present in the node's log and was applied to the FSM. The skipped entries can only have been processed by processConfigurationLogEntry, the sole writer of the tracked configuration state, and its startup caller is exactly that scan; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into r.configurations (raft.go:1605-1624). The resulting configuration state is not inert: configurations.latestIndex == 0 makes a follower refuse to start an election (raft.go:225-241), and configurations.latest supplies quorumSize, the voter set counted by checkLeaderLease, the membership map used by the leader's commitment, and the inConfiguration/hasVote admission checks for vote grants (raft.go:456-467, 1085-1094; commitment.go:35-64). Two consequences follow directly: a node with no snapshot recovers an empty configuration and can never elect itself (no reachable producer of AppendEntries or configuration entries exists in a single-voter cluster), and a node with a snapshot recovers the snapshot's older membership, including a member set that omits an entry its log already committed. The existing test for this feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration is identical to the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this case. The defect is scoped to deployments that enable RestoreCommittedLogs and use a commit-tracking log store; the intended duty is that the node recover the configuration its own log establishes, which the scan exists to do.
counterevidence: The doc comment for RestoreCommittedLogs (config.go:243-254) describes replaying committed logs to bring the FSM up to date and says nothing about configuration recovery, so one could argue that a stale configuration view is an unnamed side effect rather than a broken contract. The counter is that the scan at api.go:610-621 exists precisely to rebuild configuration state from the log at startup, and its start index is the only reason entries are skipped; no other path restores that state after the replay.

The skip also removes work: with RestoreCommittedLogs, configuration entries below the persisted commit index were already delivered to the FSM as commit tuples, so an FSM implementing ConfigurationStore has seen them. That does not restore r.configurations, which is raft's own decision input and is not derived from the FSM.
limitations: The predicate recorded here is source-derived; the fixed experiment for this question has been submitted with this batch and its retained receipt is not yet part of this account. A native local run of the same harness was used only to validate operands while constructing it and is not offered as evidence.

Both prefix cases restart a single-voter cluster on an in-memory transport with an in-memory commit-tracking log store, so the observation window (1.5s = 30 election timeouts) measures non-participation of that node, not of a multi-node cluster.

The stale-membership consequence for a leader's commit index is argued from the code path that builds the commitment from configurations.latest; no scenario in this batch partitions a multi-node cluster to show a commit decided by a member set that the committed configuration does not contain.

The persisted commit index is staged only on log writes (raft.go:1392-1405, 1553-1561), so its value in the stored prefix is not necessarily the highest committed index; this does not affect the ordering argument, since any staged value above 0 exceeds the snapshot index in these cases.

interpretations.rationale: Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c restarted four real single-voter prefixes (bootstrap, election through the normal path, client applies, shutdown) on top of their retained log, stable and snapshot stores, twice per prefix shape, with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off, and observed each restarted node for 1500ms (30 election/heartbeat timeouts at 50ms, polled every 5ms). Comparison 0 (flag on, no snapshot) is violated by witness event 2: the node ended in state Follower, leader_observed false over 268 polls, with latest_config_index 0, latest_config_ids empty and latest_config_voters 0, while the same prefix's log holds LogConfiguration@1 with one voter (event 0) and the persisted commit index was 5 (event 1). Comparison 1 (flag off, same prefix shape) holds at event 6: leader_observed true, latest_config_index 1 and latest_config_ids equal to the log's entry. Comparison 2 (flag on) is violated by witness event 3: recovered configuration index 0 with no servers against log_last_config_index 1 and log_last_config_ids carrying the single voter. Comparison 3 (flag off) holds at event 7 with config_matches_last_log_config true. Comparison 4 (flag on, snapshot at index 6 followed by a committed AddNonvoter at index 7) is violated by witness event 11: recovered latest_config_index 1 with exactly one voter and zero nonvoters (the snapshot's committed configuration, snapshot_index 6 in event 8), while the node's own log's newest configuration entry is index 7 with voters 1 and nonvoters 1 including the added peer. Comparison 5 (flag off, same prefix shape) holds at event 15 with the recovered configuration at index 7 including that peer. The controls differ from the violations only in the flag, on prefixes built the same way, so the difference tracks the replay path and not the prefix shape. Source side, the mechanism is settled: restoreFromCommittedLogs reads the persisted commit index, stores it and calls processLogs, which advances lastApplied to it (api.go:723-754), and only afterwards does NewRaft run the scan that rebuilds tracked configuration state, starting at max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied) + 1 (api.go:602-621). With the flag off lastApplied is the snapshot index and the scan covers the log; with the flag on it is the commit index, so committed configuration entries at or below it are never passed to processConfigurationLogEntry, the only writer of r.configurations (raft.go:1605-1624). The consequence recorded here is that the restarted node's decision state can be the snapshot's configuration or an empty one: with latest_config_index 0 the follower branch refuses to start an election (raft.go:225-241), which is terminal for the no-snapshot case because no reachable peer can ever send a configuration entry, and the stale view is what quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership and the vote-admission checks consume (raft.go:456-467, 1085-1094; commitment.go:35-64). Defect statement: with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a commit-tracking log store, NewRaft cannot roll the node's tracked membership configuration forward past max(snapshot index, persisted commit index), so a restarted node may keep an older or empty membership even though its log already contains the committed configuration entries; it can then be permanently unable to participate, or decide quorum from a member set that the committed configuration does not match. The duty is not documented as waived: the flag's doc comment speaks only about catching up the FSM (config.go:243-254) and says nothing about membership, while the startup scan exists precisely to rebuild that state from the log. The existing test for the feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration already equals the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this path.

98ee8dfd5fac4b84915f91ed4b094bcf-gap-0.explanation: At startup only two inputs write the tracked configuration state, in this order: restoreSnapshot copies the snapshot's committed configuration and its index into both committed and latest (api.go:645-684), and the scan at api.go:610-621 replays processConfigurationLogEntry over log indices from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 upward. The restored FSM is not a source: the ConfigurationStore interface is write-only from raft's perspective (fsm.go:110-119 invokes StoreConfiguration; nothing reads it back), so the log scan is the only input that can roll the tracked configuration forward through the log. This is corroborated by the retained receipt: in the two feature-on cases the recovered configuration was exactly the snapshot's committed configuration (event 11: index 1, one voter, no nonvoters) or the empty configuration (events 2 and 3: index 0, no servers), never the newest configuration entry in the node's own log (index 1 in the no-snapshot case per event 0, index 7 in the snapshot case per event 8).

98ee8dfd5fac4b84915f91ed4b094bcf-gap-1.explanation: Partially answered. The receipt shows one decision that the stale view changed outside the node: in the snapshot case with the flag on, the node reached leadership (event 10: final_state Leader, leader_observed true, commit_index and last_applied 10) while its tracked configuration was the snapshot's index-1 configuration with one voter and no nonvoters, not its log's committed index-7 configuration (event 11). That election was nevertheless still justifiable under the real committed configuration, because the omitted member was a nonvoter and the voting majority of both member sets is the local node, so the observed election is not yet a quorum formed from members the committed configuration excludes. A commit index advanced by a stale voter set, for example after a committed removal or a committed demotion, remains open and is not established by this receipt.

knowledge.assertion: The startup configuration scan runs from max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1, so entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry at startup.
restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the store's commit index and calls processLogs with it only when the flag is set, which advances lastApplied to that index before the scan runs.
processConfigurationLogEntry is the only writer of the tracked configuration state; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into it.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership, leader-lease voter counting and the vote-admission checks.
A follower with configurations.latestIndex equal to 0 does not start an election, which is terminal when no reachable peer can supply a configuration entry.

counterevidence: The doc comment for RestoreCommittedLogs (config.go:243-254) promises only that committed logs are replayed to catch the FSM up and says nothing about membership recovery, so the stale tracked configuration can be read as an unnamed side effect of a feature that never claimed to preserve it. The counter is that the startup scan at api.go:610-621 exists to rebuild that state from the log, and the replay merely moves its lower bound; nothing else reconstructs it afterwards.

In the snapshot case the node with the stale configuration nevertheless became leader and committed its no-op (event 10, commit_index 10), so this receipt does not show a wrong decision in that scenario: the omitted member was a nonvoter, so the majority of both the stale and the real configuration is the local node. This limits the demonstrated harm to losing a committed membership change from the node's decision state, and leaves a quorum-based violation to the open gap.

One could attribute the no-snapshot non-leadership to the observation window rather than the empty configuration. The control on the same prefix shape elected in 17 polls (about 85ms, event 6) while the feature-on node sat at 268 polls with latest_config_index 0 (event 2), and with no peers in that scenario no producer of AppendEntries or configuration entries exists, so the state cannot change on any later timescale.

Configuration entries below the persisted commit index were also delivered to the FSM as commit tuples during the replay, so an FSM implementing ConfigurationStore has observed them. That does not restore r.configurations, which is raft's own decision input and is never read back from the FSM.
limitations: All four cases restart a single-voter cluster over an in-memory transport with an in-memory commit-tracking log store; the non-participation result is about that restarted node, not about cluster availability in a multi-node deployment.

The membership difference observed in the snapshot case involves a nonvoter, so no quorum arithmetic differed between the stale and the real configuration here; the quorum consequence is argued from the code paths that consume configurations.latest and remains the open gap.
No production log store is exercised; the probe relies on a store exposing a persisted commit index, and does not verify the caller-side atomicity contract of CommitTrackingLogStore.
One prefix per case; the receipt shows schedule-independent consistency across two independent prefix constructions per shape, but not repetition of the same prefix.

The persisted commit index is staged only on log writes (raft.go:1392-1405, 1553-1561), so the value read at restart need not be the highest committed index; in these cases it is 5 and 8 respectively, both above the relevant snapshot index, which is the only ordering the argument uses.

interpretations.rationale: Source trace. With Config.RestoreCommittedLogs set, NewRaft reads the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754). processLogs walks from lastApplied+1 to that index, accumulating commit tuples and flushing a batch whenever the batch reaches config.MaxAppendEntries, delivering each batch through a select that waits for r.fsmMutateCh or r.shutdownCh (raft.go:1302-1312, 1336-1350). fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560) and is consumed only by runFSM, which NewRaft starts after the replay returns (api.go:636-638). At startup lastApplied is the restored snapshot index, so the replay spans the committed log above the snapshot, and the number of sends is ceil((commitIndex - lastApplied)/MaxAppendEntries). With the default MaxAppendEntries of 64 that is 128 sends at 8192 entries, so any restart whose committed range above the snapshot exceeds 8192 entries blocks inside NewRaft on the 129th send, with the FSM goroutine not yet started, no timeout, and no reachable way to close shutdownCh because the caller has not received the Raft object. The trigger is a legal configuration or workload: a smaller positive MaxAppendEntries lowers the bound proportionally, and a node that has never snapshotted (or whose snapshots lag its write rate) exceeds the default bound without any tuning. The failure is a startup liveness failure, not a wrong decision: the node never begins participating, so a single-voter group stays down and a larger group loses one member permanently. No repair is enabled in the blocked state: the only escape from the send is a shutdown channel that only a caller holding the returned object could close.
counterevidence: The default SnapshotThreshold of 8192 keeps the replay range near the 8192-entry bound rather than far above it, so on a fully auto-snapshotting node the block needs the range to overshoot the bound, for example because more entries were appended between the snapshot trigger and the snapshot completion. The claim does not rest on the default configuration alone: SnapshotThreshold and MaxAppendEntries are both legal config fields, and a store that keeps its log without snapshots reaches any range.

The existing feature test (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a log of about a hundred entries, far below the bound, so its passing result is not counterevidence to a bound that begins around 8192 default entries.

interpretations.rationale: Recovery. Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c restarted four real single-voter prefixes on their retained stores with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off. With the flag on and no snapshot, the node recovered an empty configuration (event 2: latest_config_index 0, no members, 268 polls with no leader) even though its log holds the bootstrap configuration entry at index 1 (event 0), while the flag-off control on the same prefix shape tracked that entry and elected itself in 17 polls (event 6); with a snapshot taken before a committed AddNonvoter, the flag-on node recovered the snapshot's index-1 configuration and never the log's committed index-7 configuration (events 10, 11), while the flag-off control recovered index 7 (event 15). Source side, the mechanism is settled: restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754), which advances lastApplied before NewRaft runs the scan that rebuilds tracked configuration state from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 (api.go:602-621); committed configuration entries at or below that bound are therefore never passed to processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go:1605-1624), and the FSM's ConfigurationStore is not read back. The tracked configuration is what decides election eligibility (raft.go:225-246), quorum size (raft.go:1085-1094), the leader's commitment membership (raft.go:456-467, commitment.go:35-64) and the vote-admission checks. Consequence, now observed. Receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a builds three voters A, B and C (event 0), snapshots A while the committed configuration is still {A,B,C} (event 1, snapshot index 4), removes C so the committed configuration becomes {A,B} at log index 5 (event 2), then restarts A with the flag on while B is partitioned and C stays connected. A's tracked configuration is the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration and it contains C (event 3: latest_config_index 1, latest_config_voters 3, latest_config_ids including C, log_config_index 5, log_config_voters 2). A then won the election - counting C's vote, a server the committed configuration no longer contains - and, in event 4, applied the client command 'stale-quorum-entry' with apply_error null at index 10 term 4, advancing its commit index and applied index to 10, while B's log does not contain that index and C's log contains it at the same term 4. A's own match index alone cannot form a majority of three, and B had no transport path to A, so the second match the commitment counted can only have come from C: the entry was committed, applied to A's FSM and reported successful to the client by a quorum that is not a majority of the committed configuration {A,B}. Defect account for the whole question: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a commit-tracking log store, NewRaft cannot roll the node's tracked membership configuration forward past max(snapshot index, persisted commit index), so a restarted node may keep an older or empty membership although its log already contains the committed configuration entries; the recovered node can then be permanently unable to participate (empty configuration), or, as observed here, decide leadership and commit index from a member set the committed configuration does not match, committing an entry that a real voter of the committed configuration does not hold. The failed predecessor execution of the multi-node experiment (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469, exit 1) is retained in the run's logs but is not cited as an execution of this interpretation: it stopped in the harness at the snapshot step with 'nothing new to snapshot' because the elected leader was not A and A had applied no entry, so it produced no comparison result about the target. The library's own test for the feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration already equals the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this path.

98ee8dfd5fac4b84915f91ed4b094bcf-gap-1.explanation: Resolved by receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a. The stale recovered configuration changed two decisions observable outside the node: the election A won (event 4, a_became_leader true) counted C, a server the committed configuration had removed, towards the majority of its tracked three-voter configuration, and the commit that followed (event 4: entry index 10, term 4, apply_error null, a_commit_index 10, a_applied_index 10, a_fsm_applied_payload true) was decided while the committed configuration's other voter B, partitioned from A, did not hold the entry (b_log_has_entry false) and the removed server C did (c_log_has_entry true, c_entry_term 4). Because A's own match cannot form a majority of three and B had no transport path to A, the second match must have come from C, so the commit rule was applied against a member set that is not a majority of the committed configuration {A,B}.

knowledge.assertion: The startup configuration scan runs from max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1, so entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry at startup.
restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the store's commit index and calls processLogs with it only when the flag is set, which advances lastApplied to that index before the scan runs.
processConfigurationLogEntry is the only writer of the tracked configuration state; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into it.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership, leader-lease voter counting and the vote-admission checks.
A follower with configurations.latestIndex equal to 0 does not start an election, which is terminal when no reachable peer can supply a configuration entry.

counterevidence: The doc comment for RestoreCommittedLogs (config.go:243-254) promises only that committed logs are replayed to catch the FSM up and says nothing about membership recovery, so the stale tracked configuration can be read as an unnamed side effect of a feature that never claimed to preserve it. The counter is that the startup scan at api.go:610-621 exists to rebuild that state from the log, and the replay merely moves its lower bound; the observed consequence is a commit decided against a member set the committed configuration does not contain.

The violating scenario needs the removed server C to stay running and reachable after its removal, since its acknowledgement is what the stale majority counted. If an operator removes a server and also stops it, or if it is unreachable, the same stale configuration would instead leave A unable to commit, so the receipt shows the reachable-removed-server case rather than every case.

The harness chose A as the restarting leader and B as the partitioned node, and it moved leadership to A with the library's leadership transfer before the snapshot; those are setup choices. They do not supply the stale configuration (event 3 shows A tracking a configuration its log had already superseded) and they do not supply the acknowledgement (C's log holds the entry at the same term), but a different assignment of roles is not exercised.

The receipt shows that the leader committed and applied the entry and returned success to the caller, and that the committed configuration's other voter lacked it; it does not follow the entry to a later term to observe an actual loss from a state machine, so the demonstrated violation is of the commitment rule rather than a completed divergence.

The first execution of the multi-node experiment failed in the harness before any comparison (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469, exit 1, 'snapshot on A failed: nothing new to snapshot'), and its single parsed event carries no configuration operands; it is retained as a harness artifact and not as evidence about the target.

The revision of that harness adds a flag-on pair at MaxAppendEntries 16: 1501 replayed entries, 94 batches, returned in 0ms (event 25, comparison holds); 3001 entries, 188 batches, did not return (event 29, comparison violated, stack naming the same frames). Receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a builds three voters at MaxAppendEntries 16, commits 3000 commands through a leader that is not A (event 9: A's staged commit index 3000, snapshot index 0, 188 batches), and restarts A in a goroutine. With the flag on the call did not return within 8000ms and the stack sample again names the replay frames (event 10), while the group kept committing with two members live (event 11: commit_while_two_live_ok true); stopping the member that is neither the leader nor A then left a single live member and the next command failed with 'leadership lost while committing log' (event 11: commit_after_stop_ok false).
