interpretations.rationale: Correction account, needed because the earlier interpretations of this question stated the reachable replay in replayed log entries. Source: processLogs appends a commit tuple only for entries prepareLog accepts - LogCommand and LogBarrier always, LogConfiguration only when protocolVersion > 2 - and none for LogNoop or the deprecated peer entries, and it flushes a batch when the batch reaches config.MaxAppendEntries (raft.go:1296-1364, prepareLog at raft.go:1364-1391). The delivered batch count is therefore ceil(tuples/MaxAppendEntries) for the tuples in the replayed range, and a count computed from the range's index span is an upper bound that can be loose when the range contains entries that produce no tuple. Corroboration from the retained boundary receipt 8a710c75d1814aafad5d24b536998539 (cited as non-supporting corroboration, since this account makes no defect judgment): the prefix whose replayed range ends at index 2049 spans 2049 entries but contains 2048 tuples, delivered as 128 batches (event 31), and NewRaft returned in 0ms (event 32); the prefix ending at 2050 contains 2049 tuples, delivered as 129 batches (event 34), and NewRaft did not return within 8000ms (event 35, three stack mentions naming the replay frames). The entry-based figure the harness computes for the returning case also reads 129 batches, which is exactly the overstatement the correction describes. What does not change: the mechanism (a full 128-slot channel whose only consumer starts after the replay returns, with no timeout), the fact that the replay is bounded by the committed range above the restored snapshot, and the consequences already recorded, since command-dominated logs deliver close to one tuple per entry. What changes: the exact threshold should be stated in delivered batches - 128 * MaxAppendEntries tuples, 8192 at the default MaxAppendEntries of 64 - and a bound stated in log entries is an upper bound rather than an equality, with the gap widening on logs that carry no-op entries or, below protocol version 3, configuration entries.

3bdf46ca8b274b719cc26e672b951e75-gap-2.explanation: The corrected unit is commit tuples. prepareLog decides it: commands and barriers always produce a tuple, configuration entries only above protocol version 2, and no-op and deprecated peer entries never do (raft.go:1364-1391), while processLogs flushes a batch when the accumulated tuples reach MaxAppendEntries (raft.go:1336-1350). So the number of sends is ceil(tuples/MaxAppendEntries), and any figure derived from a log index range is an upper bound on that number.

3bdf46ca8b274b719cc26e672b951e75-gap-3.explanation: The retained boundary receipt shows the correction in an observation rather than only in the source: a replayed range of 2049 entries ending at index 2049 held 2048 tuples and was delivered as 128 batches, and NewRaft returned in 0ms (events 31, 32), while the range ending at 2050 held 2049 tuples and 129 batches and did not return (events 34, 35). The entry-based count the harness computes reads 129 in the returning case as well, which is the overstatement the correction names.

3bdf46ca8b274b719cc26e672b951e75-gap-4.explanation: For the earlier interpretations, the change is one of precision rather than of substance: their threshold expressions in replayed entries remain upper bounds, valid where the replayed range is dominated by commands and configuration entries at protocol 3 or above, and the mechanism, the 128-slot channel, the observable block and its consequences are unaffected. The successor account for this question states the bound in delivered batches and cites the batching behaviour at revision 2, so the recorded conclusion no longer rests on the entry-based phrasing.

The correction widens in the other direction too: below protocol version 3 the replayed range can contain many configuration entries that produce no tuple, so an entry-based threshold can overstate the reachable batch count by far more than the one or two entries seen at protocol 3, while the mechanism and its consequences are unchanged.
This account makes no defect judgment of its own; the defect account for this question remains the experiment-cited interpretation, whose conclusion is unaffected by the counting unit.
limitations: The correction is supported by one source rule and one boundary receipt; no case exercises a no-op-heavy or legacy-protocol log where the entry-based and tuple-based counts diverge widely.
The earlier interpretations keep their original wording in the retained history; only their affected uses are marked, so a reader of an older account sees the entry-based phrasing.

interpretations.rationale: Correction note: this successor differs from the previous account of this question only by a transcribed latency; the control's election is now stated as the receipt records it (19 polls at a 5ms interval, about 95ms), not from an earlier construction run. Everything else - sources, executions, knowledge uses, counterevidence and limitations - is unchanged. Recovery. Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c restarted four real single-voter prefixes on their retained stores with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off: with the flag on and no snapshot the node recovered an empty configuration (event 2: no members at index 0, 268 polls without a leader) although its log holds the bootstrap configuration entry at index 1 (event 0), the flag-off control on the same prefix shape tracked that entry and elected itself (event 6), and with a snapshot taken before a committed AddNonvoter the flag-on node kept the snapshot's index-1 configuration instead of the log's committed index-7 configuration (events 10, 11) while the flag-off control recovered index 7 (event 15). Source side the mechanism is settled: restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754), advancing lastApplied before NewRaft runs the scan that rebuilds tracked configuration state from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 (api.go:602-621), so committed configuration entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go:1605-1624) and the FSM's ConfigurationStore is never read back. That state decides election eligibility (raft.go:225-246), quorum size (raft.go:1085-1094), the leader's commitment membership (raft.go:456-467, commitment.go:35-64) and vote admission. First consequence: receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a removed server C from {A,B,C} (event 2: committed configuration at index 5 with two voters), restarted A with the flag on while B was partitioned, and A tracked the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration containing C (event 3); A won the election counting C and committed 'stale-quorum-entry' at index 10 term 4 with apply_error null, its FSM applied it, B's log lacked that index and C's log held it at the same term (event 4). Since A's own match cannot form a majority of three and B had no transport path, the deciding acknowledgement can only have come from C: the entry was committed, applied and reported successful against a member set that is not a majority of the committed configuration. Second consequence, durable: receipt c477da09810f4842ba55130320e2a6b5 leaves A in that recovered state on a three-voter cluster (event 6: latest_config_index 0 with no members and committed_config_index 0, against its log's index-1 three-voter entry and staged commit index 4), takes a snapshot through the library's normal path, and reads back metadata recording no configuration at index 0 while the log establishes a three-voter configuration at index 1 (event 7, snapshot_config_matches_log_config false). A then restarts on the same stores with the replay disabled and comes up with an empty configuration at index 0, no leader within 1500ms, in state Follower (event 8). The loss is therefore not confined to the replay path: once written, the snapshot metadata re-imposes it on a restart that never enables the feature. Defect account: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a commit-tracking log store, NewRaft cannot roll the node's tracked membership configuration forward past max(snapshot index, persisted commit index), so the node may keep an older or empty membership although its own log already contains the committed configuration entries; the recovered node can be permanently unable to participate, can decide leadership and commit index from a member set the committed configuration does not match - committing an entry a real voter of that configuration does not hold - and can write the lost configuration into durable snapshot metadata, from which later restarts, including ones with the feature disabled, restore it. The library's own test for the feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration already equals the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this path. The failed first execution of the multi-node experiment (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469, exit 1) is retained in the run's logs but is not cited as an execution here: it stopped in the harness at the snapshot step because the elected leader was not the node being snapshotted, so it produced no comparison result about the target.

knowledge.assertion: The startup configuration scan runs from max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1, so entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry at startup.
restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the store's commit index and calls processLogs with it only when the flag is set, which advances lastApplied to that index before the scan runs.
processConfigurationLogEntry is the only writer of the tracked configuration state; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into it.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership, leader-lease voter counting and the vote-admission checks.
A follower with configurations.latestIndex equal to 0 does not start an election, which is terminal when no reachable peer can supply a configuration entry.
Snapshots record the committed configuration and its index that the node currently tracks, and startup restores that metadata into the tracked configuration.

counterevidence: The doc comment for RestoreCommittedLogs (config.go:243-254) promises only that committed logs are replayed to catch the FSM up and says nothing about membership recovery, so the stale tracked configuration can be read as an unnamed side effect of a feature that never claimed to preserve it. The counter is that the startup scan at api.go:610-621 exists to rebuild that state from the log, and the observed consequences are a commit decided against a member set the committed configuration does not contain and a durable record that re-imposes the loss.

The commit-rule violation needs the removed server C to stay reachable after its removal, since its acknowledgement is what the stale majority counted; if it were stopped or unreachable the same stale configuration would instead leave the node unable to commit. The receipt therefore shows one reachable-removed-server case rather than every case.

One could argue the snapshot in the durable-state case is only as good as the state the node tracks, and that a caller should not snapshot a node whose configuration is empty. The counter is that the node is an ordinary cluster member whose own log contains the configuration entries, nothing in the API or the documentation marks its snapshots as unusable, and the resulting metadata then defeats a restart that has the feature disabled, so the corruption outlives the condition that created it.

The flag-off restart's failure to lead could be attributed to the 1500ms observation window rather than to the empty configuration. The counter is the source guard that refuses elections while configurations.latestIndex is zero (raft.go:225-241), together with the control on the same prefix shape that elected itself in 19 polls of the harness's 5ms interval, about 95ms (receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c, event 6 records polls 19 and leader_observed true); 1500ms is 30 election timeouts.

The harness assigns roles deliberately (A restarts, B is partitioned, leadership is moved with the library's transfer) and it takes the snapshot explicitly rather than through the automatic cadence. Those choices select the scenario but do not supply the stale or empty configuration, which event 6 shows against the node's own log, nor the acknowledgement, which C's log carries.

The first execution of the multi-node experiment failed in the harness before any comparison (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469) and is retained as a harness artifact; the later receipts contain the same scenario with both defects exercised.
limitations: All nodes are in-memory transports and stores in one process and the harness uses a test log store whose staging is not atomic with its log writes; the caller-side durability contract of CommitTrackingLogStore is assumed, not verified, and no production store or snapshot store is exercised.

The durable-state case snapshots a node that has no snapshot on its stores and then restarts with the replay disabled; shipping such a snapshot to a follower, or corruption arising from the automatic snapshot cadence, is not exercised, and deleting the corrupt snapshot is not tested as a recovery.

The multi-node case is one prefix shape with one committed removal, keeps the removed server running, and injects no message loss, reordering or crash, so the decision defect is observed under a clean transport.

Schedule variation is limited: the multi-node scenario appears in two receipts with the same operands, the durable-state scenario in one, and the observation windows are 1500ms for non-participation and 2000ms apply timeouts.
interpretations.joint_history: All three receipts are executions of this investigation's fixed experiments on the same captured source revision, in separate workspaces with no shared mutable state. Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c established the recovery behaviour on four single-voter prefixes; receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a exercised the same recovery as the setup of a three-voter cluster and observed the commit-rule consequence; receipt c477da09810f4842ba55130320e2a6b5 contains both that three-voter scenario again (events 0-4, with the same operands: a restart tracking the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration against a log whose newest configuration entry is index 4 with two voters, and a commit at index 9 completed with only the removed server's acknowledgement) and the new durable-state scenario (events 5-8, where the same recovery leaves an empty tracked configuration). The repeated scenario reproduces the earlier witness with fresh addresses, so the premises each receipt relies on are observed more than once and the newer receipts only add consequences.

interpretations.rationale: Correction note: this successor differs from the previous account of this question only in two transcribed numbers and their attribution; the flag-off control of receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f returned in 1ms and the same control of receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 returned in 5ms, as those receipts record, and the earlier account had them swapped. Everything else - sources, executions, knowledge uses, counterevidence, limitations and joint history - is unchanged. Mechanism. With Config.RestoreCommittedLogs set, NewRaft reads the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it before starting any background goroutine (api.go:723-754). processLogs walks the committed range and appends a commit tuple only for entries prepareLog accepts - commands and barriers always, configuration entries when protocolVersion > 2, and nothing for no-op or deprecated peer entries - flushing a batch whenever the batch reaches config.MaxAppendEntries and delivering it through a select whose only other case is shutdownCh (raft.go:1296-1364 with prepareLog at raft.go:1364-1391). fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560) and its only consumer runFSM is started by api.go:636-638 after the replay returns, so a replay needing more than 128 delivered batches waits for a consumer that cannot exist until the blocked call finishes, with no timeout. Block and bound. Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f restarts a single-voter prefix holding 9001 committed entries above an absent snapshot (event 16, 141 delivered batches at MaxAppendEntries 64); the flag-on restart admitted by event 17 did not return within 8000ms (event 18, stack naming processLogs at raft.go:1346 called from restoreFromCommittedLogs at api.go:753 called from NewRaft) while the flag-off restart of the same shape returned in 1ms (event 21) and became leader (event 22); receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 reproduces both, with its own flag-off control returning in 5ms (its event 21) and adds a pair at MaxAppendEntries 16 where 1501 replayed entries (94 batches) returned in 0ms (event 25) and 3001 entries (188 batches) did not (event 29). Receipt 8a710c75d1814aafad5d24b536998539 then places the boundary exactly: at MaxAppendEntries 16 one prefix ends at staged commit index 2049, whose replayed range contains 2048 entries that become commit tuples, that is 128 delivered batches (event 31), and NewRaft returned in 0ms (event 32, comparison holds); the other ends at 2050 with 2049 tuples, that is 129 delivered batches (event 34), and NewRaft did not return within 8000ms (event 35, comparison violated, three stack mentions naming the replay frames). The pair differs only in one replayed command, so the bound is the 128-slot channel measured in delivered batches, and any count derived from the log's index range is an upper bound: the entry-based figure for the returning case also reads 129 batches (event 31), because the range includes entries that produce no tuple. Availability. Receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a builds three voters at MaxAppendEntries 16, commits 3000 commands through a leader that is not A (event 9), restarts A in a goroutine, and observes the same non-return (event 10). With the replay on the group kept committing with two members live and lost the ability after one further member was stopped (event 11: commit_while_two_live_ok true, commit_after_stop_ok false, error 'leadership lost while committing log'), while with the replay off the same stop left the pair {leader, A} live and the command succeeded (events 13, 14). The corrected unit matters for the recorded gaps: the three correction gaps ask about the premise change, and the receipt answers them substantively - the returning case's entry-based figure was 129 batches while only 128 were delivered, so counts derived from a log index range are upper bounds. Defect account: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft cannot complete startup whenever the replay delivers more than 128 batches, that is more than 128*MaxAppendEntries entries that become commit tuples above the restored snapshot index; at the default MaxAppendEntries of 64 that is 8192 tuples, and it is proportionally smaller for any smaller legal value, as measured at 16 (2048 tuples returning, 2049 blocking). The failure is a startup liveness failure: the node never begins participating, so a single-voter group stays down, a larger group runs with proportionally less fault tolerance, and one further stop was enough to make a three-voter group unable to commit. Pending operations the leader had accepted are answered with ErrLeadershipLost once it steps down (raft.go:508-528).

knowledge.assertion: Batches are counted in commit tuples, so no-op and deprecated peer entries consume no batch slot and configuration entries do so only above protocol version 2.
fsmMutateCh has capacity 128 and its consumer runFSM starts only after the startup replay returns.
The replay range above the snapshot sets the number of tuples to deliver, and the automatic snapshot cadence is the only bound on that range in a default deployment.
With the flag on, lastApplied is set to the persisted commit index before the replay, so the replay range spans the committed log above the snapshot.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize and the vote-admission checks, which is why a member that never starts is simply absent from every future majority.

counterevidence: The block itself is evidenced by non-return within an 8000ms window plus a stack sample per blocked case (events 18, 29, 10 and 35). The permanence argument does not rest on those samples: the source shows no timeout, a single consumer started only after the blocked call returns, and an escape requiring an object the caller has not received. The flag-off controls return promptly in each receipt: 1ms at event 21 of receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f, 5ms at event 21 and 0ms at event 25 of receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00, and 0ms at event 13 of receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a.

The boundary pair is a single run per side, and its delivered-tuple count is computed by the harness scanning the replayed range with the same type rule prepareLog uses rather than read from an internal counter; the behaviour itself straddles the boundary by one replayed command, and the tuple figure is an inspectable operand rather than the decisive predicate.

With the default SnapshotThreshold of 8192 equal to the default bound in tuples, a default node blocks only when the committed range above its newest snapshot exceeds 8192 tuple-producing entries; every case here raised SnapshotThreshold, a legal Config field, so how readily a default deployment crosses the bound is not measured.

The availability case contains a deliberate second stop, so what it shows is the loss of the group's fault-tolerance margin rather than an outage in an untouched cluster; the control with the replay disabled performs the same stop and still commits, which is what attributes the loss to the member that did not return.

In the flag-on availability case the surviving leader's command failed with 'leadership lost while committing log', which is the leader stepping down and failing its pending operations rather than a defect of its own; the same apply succeeded while two members were live (event 11) and after the same stop in the control (event 14).

The blocked NewRaft call is abandoned in a separate goroutine so the tests can complete; that is a harness choice, not a repair, and no harness observes the process-level consequence of a caller that waits forever.
limitations: All cases run in one process over in-memory transports and a test commit-tracking store; no production store, no process-level restart and no disk fault are exercised, and the confined goroutine is the only trace of the real caller's hang.

The availability case uses one prefix shape, one batch size (16) and one extra stop; the boundary case uses one batch size and one run per side; observation windows are 8000ms for restarts and 3000ms for the applies.
Schedule variation is limited: the original pair appears in two receipts, the bound pair, the boundary pair and the availability pair in one each, and each blocked state is sampled once.
The bound's dependence on the caller-side store is assumed rather than verified: the replay range comes from the stored commit index, whose durability contract belongs to the LogStore implementation.

Default configuration. Receipt 0cb30b6bf8874d479b83653bd4e6c553 builds two further single-voter prefixes with Config.DefaultConfig values left untouched: event 36 records SnapshotThreshold 8192, MaxAppendEntries 64, SnapshotInterval 120s, 12000 applied commands, staged commit index 12001, snapshot index 0, no snapshots listed, and a committed range of 12001 entries above the snapshot against the bound of 128*64 = 8192 tuples; the flag-on restart did not return within 8000ms with four stack samples naming the replay frames (event 38, comparison violated), while the flag-off control returned in 3ms (event 41, comparison holds). First consequence: receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a removed server C from {A,B,C} (event 2: committed configuration at index 5 with two voters), restarted A with the flag on while B was partitioned, and A tracked the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration containing C (event 3); A won the election counting C and committed 'stale-quorum-entry' at index 10 term 4 with apply_error null, its FSM applied it, B's log lacked that index and C's log held it at the same term (event 4). Since A's own match cannot form a majority of three and B had no transport path, the deciding acknowledgement can only have come from C: the entry was committed, applied and reported successful against a member set that is not a majority of the committed configuration. Authority attempt. Receipt 4178d9d5c479470cafb7ebd7951a9332 builds a three-voter group, commits three commands so the staged commit index is non-zero, restarts A over its own stores and reads its tracked configuration: with the replay enabled A tracks no configuration at all (event 15: latest_config_index 0, no members, staged commit index 4), and in 266 samples over 1500ms of hearing no leader with the other voters shut down it was a follower in every sample and never a candidate (event 16, comparison violated); with the replay disabled the same node and the same log recover the three-voter configuration (event 17: latest_config_index 1, three members) and the node was a candidate in 254 of 266 samples, ending in state Candidate (event 18, comparison holds). knowledge.assertion: The startup configuration scan runs from max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1, so entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry at startup.
restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the store's commit index and calls processLogs with it only when the flag is set, which advances lastApplied to that index before the scan runs.
processConfigurationLogEntry is the only writer of the tracked configuration state; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into it.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership, leader-lease voter counting and the vote-admission checks.
A follower with configurations.latestIndex equal to 0 does not start an election, which is terminal when no reachable peer can supply a configuration entry.
Snapshots record the committed configuration and its index that the node currently tracks, and startup restores that metadata into the tracked configuration.

counterevidence: The doc comment for RestoreCommittedLogs (config.go:243-254) promises only that committed logs are replayed to catch the FSM up and says nothing about membership recovery, so the stale tracked configuration can be read as an unnamed side effect of a feature that never claimed to preserve it. The counter is that the startup scan at api.go:610-621 exists to rebuild that state from the log, and the observed consequences are a commit decided against a member set the committed configuration does not contain and a durable record that re-imposes the loss.

The commit-rule violation needs the removed server C to stay reachable after its removal, since its acknowledgement is what the stale majority counted; if it were stopped or unreachable the same stale configuration would instead leave the node unable to commit. The receipt therefore shows one reachable-removed-server case rather than every case.

One could argue the snapshot in the durable-state case is only as good as the state the node tracks, and that a caller should not snapshot a node whose configuration is empty. The counter is that the node is an ordinary cluster member whose own log contains the configuration entries, nothing in the API or the documentation marks its snapshots as unusable, and the resulting metadata then defeats a restart that has the feature disabled, so the corruption outlives the condition that created it.

The flag-off restart's failure to lead could be attributed to the 1500ms observation window rather than to the empty configuration. The counter is the source guard that refuses elections while configurations.latestIndex is zero (raft.go:225-241) plus two controls inside the same window: the single-voter control elected itself in 19 polls of the harness's 5ms interval (receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c, event 6), and in the authority case the node that recovered its configuration was a candidate in 254 of 266 samples while the node with the empty configuration showed zero candidate samples (receipt 4178d9d5c479470cafb7ebd7951a9332, events 16 and 18).

The harness assigns roles deliberately (A restarts, B is partitioned, leadership is moved with the library's transfer) and it takes the snapshot explicitly rather than through the automatic cadence. Those choices select the scenario but do not supply the stale or empty configuration, which event 6 shows against the node's own log, nor the acknowledgement, which C's log carries.

The first execution of the multi-node experiment failed in the harness before any comparison (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469) and is retained as a harness artifact; the later receipts contain the same scenario with both defects exercised.

The authority case removes the other voters by shutting them down, so it shows that the defective node never attempts candidacy; it does not show an outage that a correct recovery would have prevented, because the recovered three-voter configuration also lacks a quorum with one voter left. The authority witness depends on a property of the caller's store: A's persisted commit index must be non-zero, because that value becomes lastApplied and pushes the startup scan above the log's configuration entry. The durable-state case snapshots a node that has no snapshot on its stores and then restarts with the replay disabled; shipping such a snapshot to a follower, or corruption arising from the automatic snapshot cadence, is not exercised, and deleting the corrupt snapshot is not tested as a recovery.

Schedule variation is limited: the multi-node scenario appears in two receipts with the same operands, the durable-state scenario in one, and the observation windows are 1500ms for non-participation and 2000ms apply timeouts.

The authority witness has one execution in which its premise held and one repeat in which it did not, so it is currently a single valid witness; a revised experiment that keeps committing until A's persisted commit index is non-zero was submitted with this batch and its receipt is not yet part of this account.

Precision note: the entry-based batch figures recorded by the earlier receipts equal the delivered counts there, and the receipts' own operands show why. In receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f event 16 the prefix ends at log index 9002 with staged commit index 9001, so the replayed range holds the bootstrap configuration entry, one no-op and 8999 commands, that is 9000 tuples, and ceil(9000/64) = 141, the figure the receipt records for that case. Receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 records 1501 and 3001 replayed entries with 94 and 188 batches at MaxAppendEntries 16, and the same counting gives 1500 and 3000 tuples, ceil(1500/16) = 94 and ceil(3000/16) = 188. With Config.RestoreCommittedLogs set, NewRaft reads the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it before starting any background goroutine (api.go:723-754). processLogs walks the committed range and appends a commit tuple only for entries prepareLog accepts - commands and barriers always, configuration entries when protocolVersion > 2, and nothing for no-op or deprecated peer entries - flushing a batch whenever the batch reaches config.MaxAppendEntries and delivering it through a select whose only other case is shutdownCh (raft.go:1296-1364 with prepareLog at raft.go:1364-1391). fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560) and its only consumer runFSM is started by api.go:636-638 after the replay returns, so a replay needing more than 128 delivered batches waits for a consumer that cannot exist until the blocked call finishes, with no timeout. Block and bound. Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f restarts a single-voter prefix holding 9001 committed entries above an absent snapshot (event 16, 141 delivered batches at MaxAppendEntries 64); the flag-on restart admitted by event 17 did not return within 8000ms (event 18, stack naming processLogs at raft.go:1346 called from restoreFromCommittedLogs at api.go:753 called from NewRaft) while the flag-off restart of the same shape returned in 1ms (event 21) and became leader (event 22); receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 reproduces both, with its own flag-off control returning in 5ms (its event 21) and adds a pair at MaxAppendEntries 16 where 1501 replayed entries (94 batches) returned in 0ms (event 25) and 3001 entries (188 batches) did not (event 29). Receipt 8a710c75d1814aafad5d24b536998539 then places the boundary exactly: at MaxAppendEntries 16 one prefix ends at staged commit index 2049, whose replayed range contains 2048 entries that become commit tuples, that is 128 delivered batches (event 31), and NewRaft returned in 0ms (event 32, comparison holds); the other ends at 2050 with 2049 tuples, that is 129 delivered batches (event 34), and NewRaft did not return within 8000ms (event 35, comparison violated, three stack mentions naming the replay frames). Receipt 0cb30b6bf8874d479b83653bd4e6c553 builds two further single-voter prefixes with Config.DefaultConfig values left untouched: event 36 records SnapshotThreshold 8192, MaxAppendEntries 64, SnapshotInterval 120s, 12000 applied commands, staged commit index 12001, snapshot index 0, no snapshots listed, and a committed range of 12001 entries above the snapshot against the bound of 128*64 = 8192 tuples; the flag-on restart did not return within 8000ms with four stack samples naming the replay frames (event 38, comparison violated), while the flag-off control returned in 3ms (event 41, comparison holds). Receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a builds three voters at MaxAppendEntries 16, commits 3000 commands through a leader that is not A (event 9), restarts A in a goroutine, and observes the same non-return (event 10). knowledge.assertion: Batches are counted in commit tuples, so no-op and deprecated peer entries consume no batch slot and configuration entries do so only above protocol version 2.
fsmMutateCh has capacity 128 and its consumer runFSM starts only after the startup replay returns.
The replay range above the snapshot sets the number of tuples to deliver, and the automatic snapshot cadence is the only bound on that range in a default deployment.
With the flag on, lastApplied is set to the persisted commit index before the replay, so the replay range spans the committed log above the snapshot.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize and the vote-admission checks, which is why a member that never starts is simply absent from every future majority.

counterevidence: The block itself is evidenced by non-return within an 8000ms window plus a stack sample per blocked case (events 18, 29, 10 and 35). The permanence argument does not rest on those samples: the source shows no timeout, a single consumer started only after the blocked call returns, and an escape requiring an object the caller has not received. The flag-off controls return promptly in each receipt: 1ms at event 21 of receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f, 5ms at event 21 and 0ms at event 25 of receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00, and 0ms at event 13 of receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a.

The boundary pair has now been executed twice from the same fixed inputs in separate clean copies with identical operands (receipts 8a710c75d1814aafad5d24b536998539 and 9039d268ffc24fa085efc75de7dc4fb2), but its delivered-tuple count is computed by the harness scanning the replayed range with the same type rule prepareLog uses rather than read from an internal counter; the behaviour straddles the boundary by one replayed command, and the tuple figure is an inspectable operand rather than the decisive predicate.

The default-configuration case is a burst: the harness applies commands as fast as the in-memory stack allows and no automatic snapshot had fired at restart (event 36: snapshot index 0, no snapshots listed). It reproduced identically in the second execution of the same fixed experiment (receipt 9039d268ffc24fa085efc75de7dc4fb2, events 36 to 41). The availability case contains a deliberate second stop, so what it shows is the loss of the group's fault-tolerance margin rather than an outage in an untouched cluster; the control with the replay disabled performs the same stop and still commits, which is what attributes the loss to the member that did not return.

In the flag-on availability case the surviving leader's command failed with 'leadership lost while committing log', which is the leader stepping down and failing its pending operations rather than a defect of its own; the same apply succeeded while two members were live (event 11) and after the same stop in the control (event 14).

The blocked NewRaft call is abandoned in a separate goroutine so the tests can complete; that is a harness choice, not a repair, and no harness observes the process-level consequence of a caller that waits forever.
limitations: All cases run in one process over in-memory transports and a test commit-tracking store; no production store, no process-level restart and no disk fault are exercised, and the confined goroutine is the only trace of the real caller's hang.

Schedule variation is unevenly covered: the original 9000-entry pair appears in two receipts, the boundary pair and the default-configuration pair have each been executed twice from the same fixed inputs with identical operands, while the bound pair remains single-run and the availability pair has now been executed three times with the same split; each blocked state is still sampled once per execution.

With Config.RestoreCommittedLogs set, NewRaft reads the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it before starting any background goroutine (api.go:723-754). processLogs walks the committed range and appends a commit tuple only for entries prepareLog accepts - commands and barriers always, configuration entries when protocolVersion > 2, and nothing for no-op or deprecated peer entries - flushing a batch whenever the batch reaches config.MaxAppendEntries and delivering it through a select whose only other case is shutdownCh (raft.go:1296-1364 with prepareLog at raft.go:1364-1391). fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560) and its only consumer runFSM is started by api.go:636-638 after the replay returns, so a replay needing more than 128 delivered batches waits for a consumer that cannot exist until the blocked call finishes, with no timeout. Block and bound. Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f restarts a single-voter prefix holding 9001 committed entries above an absent snapshot (event 16, 141 delivered batches at MaxAppendEntries 64); the flag-on restart admitted by event 17 did not return within 8000ms (event 18, stack naming processLogs at raft.go:1346 called from restoreFromCommittedLogs at api.go:753 called from NewRaft) while the flag-off restart of the same shape returned in 1ms (event 21) and became leader (event 22); receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 reproduces both, with its own flag-off control returning in 5ms (its event 21) and adds a pair at MaxAppendEntries 16 where 1501 replayed entries (94 batches) returned in 0ms (event 25) and 3001 entries (188 batches) did not (event 29). Receipt 8a710c75d1814aafad5d24b536998539 then places the boundary exactly: at MaxAppendEntries 16 one prefix ends at staged commit index 2049, whose replayed range contains 2048 entries that become commit tuples, that is 128 delivered batches (event 31), and NewRaft returned in 0ms (event 32, comparison holds); the other ends at 2050 with 2049 tuples, that is 129 delivered batches (event 34), and NewRaft did not return within 8000ms (event 35, comparison violated, three stack mentions naming the replay frames). The pair differs only in one replayed command, so the bound is the 128-slot channel measured in delivered batches, and any count derived from the log's index range is an upper bound: the entry-based figure for the returning case also reads 129 batches (event 31), because the range includes entries that produce no tuple. Default configuration. Receipt 0cb30b6bf8874d479b83653bd4e6c553 builds two further single-voter prefixes with Config.DefaultConfig values left untouched: event 36 records SnapshotThreshold 8192, MaxAppendEntries 64, SnapshotInterval 120s, 12000 applied commands, staged commit index 12001, snapshot index 0, no snapshots listed, and a committed range of 12001 entries above the snapshot against the bound of 128*64 = 8192 tuples; the flag-on restart did not return within 8000ms with four stack samples naming the replay frames (event 38, comparison violated), while the flag-off control returned in 3ms (event 41, comparison holds). The trigger therefore needs no tuning of threshold or batch size: the automatic snapshot loop wakes on a randomized timeout of up to SnapshotInterval (snapshot.go:71-95), so a node that commits faster than that cadence carries a range above the bound into its restart. Availability. Receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a builds three voters at MaxAppendEntries 16, commits 3000 commands through a leader that is not A (event 9), restarts A in a goroutine, and observes the same non-return (event 10). With the replay on the group kept committing with two members live and lost the ability after one further member was stopped (event 11: commit_while_two_live_ok true, commit_after_stop_ok false, error 'leadership lost while committing log'), while with the replay off the same stop left the pair {leader, A} live and the command succeeded (events 13, 14). That pair reproduced identically in two later executions of the same harness (receipts fe822d82c6264158826e0303b4ce59b1 and 67fc59b525e54d01b709a19592689357, events 9 to 14 in each: staged commit index 3001 with the replay enabled and 3000 with it disabled, the replay-enabled restart not returning, the group committing with two members live and losing the ability after the second stop, and the control returning in 0ms and committing), so the availability consequence now rests on three executions with the same split. The corrected unit matters for the recorded gaps: the three correction gaps ask about the premise change, and the receipt answers them substantively - the returning case's entry-based figure was 129 batches while only 128 were delivered, so counts derived from a log index range are upper bounds. Defect account: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft cannot complete startup whenever the replay delivers more than 128 batches, that is more than 128*MaxAppendEntries entries that become commit tuples above the restored snapshot index; at the default MaxAppendEntries of 64 that is 8192 tuples, and it is proportionally smaller for any smaller legal value, as measured at 16 (2048 tuples returning, 2049 blocking). The failure is a startup liveness failure: the node never begins participating, so a single-voter group stays down, a larger group runs with proportionally less fault tolerance, and one further stop was enough to make a three-voter group unable to commit. Pending operations the leader had accepted are answered with ErrLeadershipLost once it steps down (raft.go:508-528). Reproducibility of the bound pair: receipt 962196ed81fd46cfb9476bbd63c2c637 is a second execution of the same fixed experiment and returns the same operands as receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 - events 23 and 25 record 1501 replayed entries with 94 batches and a return in 0ms, events 27 and 29 record 3001 entries with 188 batches and no return with the replay frames in the stack, and the only differing operand is the flag-off control's return latency, 5ms then 3ms.

knowledge.assertion: Batches are counted in commit tuples, so no-op and deprecated peer entries consume no batch slot and configuration entries do so only above protocol version 2.
fsmMutateCh has capacity 128 and its consumer runFSM starts only after the startup replay returns.

The snapshot check is only evaluated when a randomized timeout of up to SnapshotInterval expires, so the committed range above the newest snapshot can exceed SnapshotThreshold by a wide margin between checks.
With the flag on, lastApplied is set to the persisted commit index before the replay, so the replay range spans the committed log above the snapshot.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize and the vote-admission checks, which is why a member that never starts is simply absent from every future majority.

counterevidence: The block itself is evidenced by non-return within an 8000ms window plus a stack sample per blocked case (events 18, 29, 10 and 35). The permanence argument does not rest on those samples: the source shows no timeout, a single consumer started only after the blocked call returns, and an escape requiring an object the caller has not received. The flag-off controls return promptly in each receipt: 1ms at event 21 of receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f, 5ms at event 21 and 0ms at event 25 of receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00, and 0ms at event 13 of receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a.

The boundary pair has now been executed twice from the same fixed inputs in separate clean copies with identical operands (receipts 8a710c75d1814aafad5d24b536998539 and 9039d268ffc24fa085efc75de7dc4fb2), but its delivered-tuple count is computed by the harness scanning the replayed range with the same type rule prepareLog uses rather than read from an internal counter; the behaviour straddles the boundary by one replayed command, and the tuple figure is an inspectable operand rather than the decisive predicate.

The default-configuration case is a burst: the harness applies commands as fast as the in-memory stack allows and no automatic snapshot had fired at restart (event 36: snapshot index 0, no snapshots listed). It reproduced identically in the second execution of the same fixed experiment (receipt 9039d268ffc24fa085efc75de7dc4fb2, events 36 to 41). It shows that default settings do not keep the range below the bound during a burst, not how long a node typically stays above it, and the other cases that raised SnapshotThreshold made the condition permanent rather than momentary.

The availability case contains a deliberate second stop, so what it shows is the loss of the group's fault-tolerance margin rather than an outage in an untouched cluster; the control with the replay disabled performs the same stop and still commits, which is what attributes the loss to the member that did not return.

In the flag-on availability case the surviving leader's command failed with 'leadership lost while committing log', which is the leader stepping down and failing its pending operations rather than a defect of its own; the same apply succeeded while two members were live (event 11) and after the same stop in the control (event 14).

The blocked NewRaft call is abandoned in a separate goroutine so the tests can complete; that is a harness choice, not a repair, and no harness observes the process-level consequence of a caller that waits forever.
limitations: All cases run in one process over in-memory transports and a test commit-tracking store; no production store, no process-level restart and no disk fault are exercised, and the confined goroutine is the only trace of the real caller's hang.

The availability case uses one prefix shape, one batch size (16) and one extra stop; the boundary case uses one batch size and one run per side; observation windows are 8000ms for restarts and 3000ms for the applies.

Schedule variation is unevenly covered: the original 9000-entry pair appears in two receipts, the boundary pair and the default-configuration pair have each been executed twice from the same fixed inputs with identical operands, the bound pair has now been executed twice with identical operands, and the availability pair three times with the same split; each blocked state is still sampled once per execution.
The bound's dependence on the caller-side store is assumed rather than verified: the replay range comes from the stored commit index, whose durability contract belongs to the LogStore implementation.
interpretations.joint_history: All four receipts are executions of fixed experiments for this investigation on the same captured source revision, in separate workspaces with no shared mutable state, and their harnesses share the same initialization: an in-memory commit-tracking log store, a single-voter bootstrap for the first three, RestoreCommittedLogs enabled on the prefix, and the restart in a separate goroutine with an 8000ms window. Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f and its revision e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 use one harness whose cases differ only in Config.MaxAppendEntries and the committed range, and e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 re-runs the original 9000-entry pair unchanged. Receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a uses a three-voter harness at the same MaxAppendEntries 16 and observes the same block. Receipt 8a710c75d1814aafad5d24b536998539 uses the first harness's prefix construction with targets chosen from an earlier construction run of the same case and places the replay on both sides of the channel capacity. The blocked state in every receipt is corroborated by a stack sample naming the replay frames, and no receipt depends on another's runtime state. Receipt 9039d268ffc24fa085efc75de7dc4fb2 is not a separate producer at all: it is the same fixed experiment as receipt 0cb30b6bf8874d479b83653bd4e6c553 executed a second time in a fresh clean copy, which is why its events carry the same names and indices. Receipt 0cb30b6bf8874d479b83653bd4e6c553 uses the same single-voter prefix construction with Config.DefaultConfig left in place for the snapshot settings, so its operands (staged commit index, snapshot index, replay batches) are directly comparable with the earlier receipts' fields of the same names. Two further receipts are shared with the configuration-recovery investigation: fe822d82c6264158826e0303b4ce59b1 and 67fc59b525e54d01b709a19592689357 are executions of that investigation's multi-node harness, which contains the availability case alongside its own cases, so their events 9 to 14 are the same case this investigation's receipt ebb3bb9fa26547f790129eea909d1d5a recorded, re-observed under the same fixed inputs. Receipt 962196ed81fd46cfb9476bbd63c2c637 is the same fixed experiment as receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 executed a second time in a fresh clean copy, which is why their events carry the same names and indices and only the flag-off return latencies differ (5ms and 3ms).
